messages.subject: Re: Order status L-49092
messages.text:
Hi Thom,

Good news first: if nothing has come up after this long, we'll reship your seeds at no charge, so you won't be stuck with that patch of expensive nothing.

A. syriaca planted on April 29 in Southern California is actually a tricky combination. Common milkweed has a fairly strong dormancy, and in a warm climate where the soil temperature never really drops, germination can be slow or uneven even with cold stratification done beforehand. A few things worth checking:

- How deep are they planted? A. syriaca should be no more than 5 mm under the surface, any deeper and they really struggle to break through.
- Is the spot getting full sun? Common milkweed does best with at least 6 hours of direct sun.
- Have nighttime temperatures been consistently above 15 to 18°C? That's usually when they start to move.

Either way, I'd rather just send you a fresh batch. Is the shipping address still the same one on your original order? Once you confirm, we'll get it out to you.

One note: if you want a better shot at germination in a warm climate, A. incarnata (swamp milkweed) tends to be a bit easier to establish than syriaca. Happy to send that instead, or a mix, just let us know.

Warmly,
__
 Gabriel Gouveia 
Co-founder
Lasclay.com

messages.subject: Re: My seeds
messages.text:
Hi Thom,
 You said yes on July 16 and then heard nothing for six weeks. That is on us, and I am sorry — especially after you had already written twice.
 Your five packets of cold-stratified A. syriaca ship this week , to the same Claremont address, at no charge. Stock is confirmed, so nothing is holding it up.
 And your question, which deserved an answer: yes, the paper towel method is worth doing , and in Southern California I would recommend it. Damp paper towel, sealed bag, in the fridge for two to three weeks, then check every few days. Plant each seed as soon as you see the root tip emerge — do not wait for the whole batch. It lets you sow only the seeds you know are viable, instead of trusting soil temperatures that never really drop where you are.
 One adjustment for your climate: sow in late fall rather than spring. Syriaca wants the cold cue, and your winter is the closest thing it will get.
 Warmly,
__
 Gabriel Gouveia 
Co-founder
Lasclay.com
 This message was drafted with the help of an AI assistant and reviewed by our team.
